[2026] FWC 218.outcome: Only the valid-reason test recitation at [28], [30], [31] was read and confirmed. This decision's own finding on Mr Potter's case was not read in this pass — not asserted here.

[2023] FWC 65.short_name: 25 employees v DP World Sydney & Brisbane
[2023] FWC 65.outcome: Cited here only for its restatement of the Sydney Trains v Hilder principles at [36]; this case's own outcome is not relied on and not asserted.

[2021] FWC 13.short_name: Hijazi v Calvary Health Care ACT
[2021] FWC 13.outcome: Valid reason found related to conduct — confirmed at [91]. The finding relied on the employee's own concessions, with limited reliance on the investigation report — confirmed at [92].

[2023] FWC 961.outcome: Application dismissed — not unfair. Conduct (a slap) found proven on the balance of probabilities, with Briginshaw considerations applied at [42]-[45]; final order at [58].

[2021] FWC 5677.outcome: Only the policy-breach principle (quoting B, C and D v Australian Postal Corporation) and the lawful-and-reasonable-direction test were read and confirmed at [12]-[13]. This decision's own finding on Ms Desmond's case was not read in this pass — not asserted here.

[2021] FWC 3122.outcome: Cited only for the meaning of "capacity" under s.387(a), confirmed at [74]. This case's own outcome is not relied on and not asserted.

[2025] FWC 3137.outcome: Valid reason found related to capacity (sustained underperformance against measured targets, despite training and two improvement plans) — confirmed at [84].

[2022] FWC 326.outcome: Only the out-of-hours-conduct test (Rose v Telstra, as applied) was read and confirmed at [54]-[55]. This decision's own finding on Mr Ronchi's case was not read in this pass — not asserted here.

[2022] FWC 2368.short_name: Elliott v Care for Kids Group
[2022] FWC 2368.outcome: No valid reason found — confirmed at [56]. The dismissal was based on an arrangement about her parents' employment, not anything the employee did — confirmed at [53]-[55]. Compensation was subsequently calculated (paragraphs beyond [99], not independently re-read here).

[2023] FWC 3367.outcome: No valid reason found — confirmed at [60]. The allegation that Mr Vetiyatil knowingly lodged false ATO reports was not made out; he genuinely believed the reports were correct — confirmed at [58]-[59].

[2023] FWC 2758.outcome: Confirmed at [99]-[100]: the employer did not check that the information behind its site-access policy was still current, undermining the direction's reasonableness. This decision's final finding on valid reason was not read in this pass — not asserted here.

[2020] FWC 5506.outcome: Only the full text of s.382 at [20], and the parties' common ground at [4] that Mr Rogers met the minimum employment period but earned above the high income threshold, were read and confirmed. This decision's own finding on whether a modern award covered Mr Rogers (the point actually in dispute) was not read in this pass — not asserted here.

[2022] FWC 2033.short_name: Mulipola v Hays Specialist Recruitment / Department of Veterans' Affairs
[2022] FWC 2033.outcome: Application failed — Mr Mulipola had not served the minimum employment period under s.383 with either Hays or the Department of Veterans' Affairs, confirmed at [79]. His casual engagement at DVA lasted only 7 weeks and 1 day and did not meet the regular-and-systematic exception in s.384(2)(a), confirmed at [29] and [77].

[2022] FWC 338.outcome: Jurisdictional objection upheld, application dismissed — Ms Johnson's annual rate of earnings (salary plus the value of a company vehicle, health cover and mobile phone/data, calculated under s.332) exceeded the high income threshold applicable at the date of her dismissal ($153,600), and she was not covered by a modern award or enterprise agreement — confirmed at [107].

[2023] FWC 2405.outcome: Found that the application was made within the 21-day period required by s.394(2)(a); in the alternative, time was extended under s.394(2)(b)/(3) on the basis that exceptional circumstances were established — confirmed at [21].

[2021] FWC 3903.outcome: Extension of time refused and application dismissed — the Commission was not satisfied there were exceptional circumstances under s.394(3), even taking into account the applicant's evidence of a poor mental state following her dismissal, either individually or in combination — confirmed at [54].

[2023] FWC 2493.short_name: Pewsukngem v Choc Dee Thai Restaurant
[2023] FWC 2493.outcome: The jurisdictional objection that the dismissal was consistent with the Small Business Fair Dismissal Code was not upheld — the employer did not establish reasonable grounds for its belief that the conduct justified summary dismissal, confirmed at [135]-[136]. This is the jurisdictional ruling only; the Commission's later s.387 finding on harshness was not read in this pass and is not asserted here.

[2021] FWC 928.outcome: Dismissal found to be a case of genuine redundancy under s.389 — the Respondent no longer required the role, had no consultation obligation because no award or agreement applied, and redeployment was not reasonable in the circumstances — confirmed at [228]. Application accordingly barred from proceeding to a harshness assessment — confirmed at [229].

[2021] FWC 3264.short_name: Baxter v Surfside Buslines Pty Ltd
[2021] FWC 3264.outcome: General protections dismissal application dismissed — the Commission concluded at [158] that the dismissal did not contravene the general protections provisions. Cited mainly for its recitation at [15] of the Keep v Performance Automobiles s.340 test (workplace right / adverse action / because of a prohibited reason, and the substantial-and-operative-factor test) and at [17] of the Tattsbet v Morrow objective-fact requirement before the s.361 onus engages.

[2024] FWC 2475.short_name: Hastings v Platform To Pty Ltd
[2024] FWC 2475.outcome: Application dismissed — confirmed at [50]. The applicant alleged dismissal because she exercised a workplace right (s.340) and because of her disability, Autism Spectrum Disorder (s.351). Adverse action (dismissal) was not disputed at [40]. The two decision-makers gave specific, consistent, first-hand evidence of the actual operational and conduct-based reasons for the dismissal, which the Commission accepted discharged the s.361 reverse onus — confirmed at [43], [47]-[49].

[2024] FWC 840.short_name: Yoon v Go Travelling Pty Ltd
[2024] FWC 840.outcome: Application dismissed — confirmed at [33]. The applicant exercised a workplace right under s.341(1)(c) by inquiring about study-leave pay entitlements; dismissal was adverse action (not disputed, [26]). The decision-maker (Ms Tong) gave evidence, accepted as consistent and credible, that the real reason was the respondent's financial position, discharging the s.361 reverse onus — confirmed at [29]-[30], [33].

[2025] FWC 777.short_name: Gray v Rim Fire Asia Pacific Pty Ltd
[2025] FWC 777.outcome: The Commission found the adverse action (dismissal) was taken for protected reasons — confirmed at [31]: the applicant's workplace complaint about a co-worker (s.341(1)(c)(ii)) and his disclosure of a pre-existing medical condition (s.351). The respondent's actual decision-maker did not give evidence or a witness statement; the witness who did appear gave only unsupported verbal submissions about a redundancy rationale, which the Commission found did not discharge the s.361 reverse onus — confirmed at [26]-[30]. Remedy was left to a further directions process, confirmed at [32] — the remedy itself was not read in this pass.

[2026] FWC 1138.short_name: Loy v Indigo Lawyers Pty Ltd
[2026] FWC 1138.outcome: Application dismissed — confirmed at [29]-[30]. The applicant alleged dismissal for exercising a workplace right but, after being granted an extension of time, failed to file any evidence or submissions despite repeated directions and warnings. The Commission held that because there was no evidence she exercised a workplace right, it was unnecessary for the respondent to discharge the s.361 reverse onus at all — confirmed at [26]-[28]. Clean illustration that the presumption only engages once the applicant proves the underlying facts.

[2026] FWC 1685.short_name: Hibbet v Cowra Meat Processors Pty Ltd
[2026] FWC 1685.outcome: Application dismissed for want of jurisdiction — confirmed at [49]: the applicant, a casual employee not offered further shifts, was found not to have been "dismissed" within the meaning of s.386(1)(a) at all. The Commission expressly distinguished the s.361 reverse onus (which would apply to the reason for an adverse action) from the separate, un-reversed onus on the applicant to first prove the jurisdictional fact of dismissal — confirmed at [45]. The merits of the applicant's workplace-right allegation (an overtime complaint) were not reached.

[2023] FWC 806.short_name: Maritime Union of Australia v DP World Brisbane Pty Ltd
[2023] FWC 806.outcome: This is an enterprise-agreement dispute-resolution decision about the construction of a right-of-representation clause, not a general protections adverse-action case. Cited here only for the accurate paraphrase of s.346 and s.347(a)/(b) recorded as part of the employer's submission at [96] (itself unchallenged as a statement of the general protections scheme) — not relied on for, and not asserting anything about, this decision's own ruling on the enterprise agreement clause.

[2024] FWC 2822.short_name: Olsen v Lynas Services Pty Ltd
[2024] FWC 2822.outcome: This decision resolves only an extension-of-time application under s.366(2); the Commission found exceptional circumstances and extended time to 4 August 2024, confirmed at [93]-[94]. The s.351(1) test (adverse action because of a protected attribute, here political opinion) and the s.351(2)-(3) anti-discrimination-law carve-out, read at [83]-[84], were considered only as part of the preliminary "merits" factor in the extension-of-time test. The substantive general protections discrimination claim itself was not decided in this decision and was not read in this pass.

[2023] FWC 991.short_name: Cloutte v S & S Webster Investments
[2023] FWC 991.outcome: Valid reason for dismissal found (failure to comply with a lawful and reasonable COVID-19 vaccination direction) — confirmed at [100]. The dismissal was found not harsh, unjust or unreasonable and the application was dismissed — confirmed at [109]. The Commission separately held the Vaccination Policy was not incorporated as a term of the Applicant's contract of employment, rejecting the Applicant's breach-of-contract argument — confirmed at [85]-[86].

[2022] FWC 2527.outcome: Dismissal found unfair — confirmed at [68] (no valid reason, and in any event disproportionate/harsh). The enterprise agreement's disciplinary procedure was mandatory once engaged and the employer's failure to follow it was a relevant, additional matter under s.387(h) — confirmed at [60], [63]. Remedy was reinstatement — confirmed at [69] (only the threshold 'reinstatement is appropriate' finding was read; the full remedy order terms beyond that were not independently re-read in this pass).

[2021] FWC 4526.outcome: A s.739 agreement dispute about pay-point progression for Works Delivery Coordinators, not an unfair dismissal matter. The Commission determined that the enterprise agreement does not mandate or entitle the relevant employees to progress through the disputed pay points without the additional qualification in issue — confirmed at [27]. Cited in this module only for its statement that the employer's performance-management policy was not incorporated into the agreement and so created no enforceable term or right — confirmed at [19].

[2025] FWC 702.outcome: Dismissal found harsh and unreasonable, with compensation ordered — confirmed at [178]-[179]. There was a valid reason related to capacity (loss of site access and no suitable alternative role), but the employer's mischaracterisation of the matter as 'serious misconduct' under its own Disciplinary Procedure, and its failure to manage performance/attendance concerns in accordance with that Procedure, the contract and the enterprise agreement, made the dismissal harsh — confirmed at [6], [85], [178].

[2022] FWC 1273.outcome: Application dismissed — dismissal not harsh, unjust or unreasonable, confirmed at [53]. The Commission found Mr Benamar's repeated refusal to comply with a lawful vaccination direction was serious misconduct within the meaning of reg 1.07, so no notice or payment in lieu was required under ss.117/123 — confirmed at [46]-[47].

[2024] FWC 2513.outcome: Application dismissed — not satisfied the Applicant was unfairly dismissed, confirmed at [71]. The Commission found Mr Xu's conduct (broadcasting unsubstantiated allegations against senior colleagues by email and WeChat) met the reg 1.07 definition of serious misconduct and established a valid reason for dismissal — confirmed at [51].

[2021] FWC 6693.outcome: Dismissal found harsh, and therefore unfair, confirmed at [48]: Mr Chebbo's conduct (attending a protest in breach of stay-at-home orders and a direction to go home) gave the employer a valid reason to dismiss him, but did not meet the reg 1.07 threshold for serious misconduct, so he should have been dismissed on notice rather than summarily. Compensation was ordered equivalent to the notice period he was denied (4 weeks' pay) — confirmed at [49].

[2024] FWC 913.short_name: Campbell v Gold Tiger Logistics Qld
[2024] FWC 913.outcome: Dismissal found unfair, confirmed at [106]. The Commission found there was no valid reason for the dismissal at all — confirmed at [87] — and separately that Ms Campbell was dismissed with immediate effect and given no notice period — confirmed at [95].

[2024] FWC 3291.short_name: Black v Baker Heart and Diabetes Institute
[2024] FWC 3291.outcome: Dismissal found unreasonable (no valid reason) and harsh, confirmed at [72]: characterising Mrs Black's conduct as serious misconduct warranting summary dismissal was a disproportionate response. Compensation (not reinstatement) was found appropriate in principle at [74], but the Commission deferred the final amount pending updated particulars — that further remedy material was not read in this pass, so it is not asserted here.

[2024] FWC 1685.outcome: Dismissal found harsh, unjust and unreasonable — confirmed at [50]. The Commission found no valid reason for dismissal at [28], and separately that the alternate reasons the employer later relied on (raised for the first time in its Form F3 employer response) were not notified to the Applicant until after the dismissal, and that he was given no opportunity at all to respond to the termination letter — confirmed at [36]-[37]. Compensation of $27,707.66 was ordered — confirmed at [49], [51].

[2023] FWC 3059.short_name: Hickey v Mt Alexander Timber & Hardware
[2023] FWC 3059.outcome: Dismissal found not harsh, unjust or unreasonable overall — confirmed at [90]. The Commission accepted the Applicant's submission that the employer was "going through the motions" of giving him an opportunity to respond during the show cause process when a decision to end his employment had, in substance, already been made — confirmed at [73], and that this procedural defect weighed in the Applicant's favour — confirmed at [91]. However, the Commission found this was outweighed by a valid reason (dishonesty during the show cause process) — confirmed at [90]-[91]. Illustrates that a genuine s.387(b)/(c) failure does not automatically make a dismissal unfair.

[2024] FWC 3017.outcome: Both dismissals found unfair — confirmed at [52]. The applicants (employees of a 4WD parts and accessories retailer) were not notified of the valid reason for their dismissal (the closure of their store) prior to the dismissal taking effect, and were given no proper opportunity to respond — confirmed at [41], [43]. A small amount of compensation (24 hours' pay each) was ordered — confirmed at [61].

[2022] FWC 1576.short_name: Kazantzis & Ors v Patrick Stevedores Holdings
[2022] FWC 1576.outcome: All applications dismissed (not unfair) — confirmed at [103]. Among other findings, the Commission found that standard-form show cause letters issued to each applicant (stevedores, straddle operators and a senior clerk dismissed for failing to comply with a COVID-19 vaccination requirement) notified each of them of the proposed reason for dismissal and gave each of them an adequate opportunity to respond — confirmed at [95]. Used here only for that s.387(b)/(c) finding; the vaccination-mandate reasoning itself is not relied on.

[2022] FWC 3249.outcome: Application dismissed. On s.387(d): excluding Mr Laalaa from PIP meetings as the Applicant's support person (because he was disruptive and tried to advocate the Applicant's case) was not an unreasonable refusal; the Commissioner treated the factor as weighing neutrally overall.

[2024] FWC 953.short_name: Nuttall v BM Supplies Unit Trust
[2024] FWC 953.outcome: Found to have been unfairly dismissed. On s.387(d): no refusal arose because the Applicant never requested a support person — there were no discussions relating to the dismissal before the phone call that terminated him.

[2026] FWC 75.short_name: Riley v Nuvei Australia Merchant Services
[2026] FWC 75.outcome: Found not to have been unfairly dismissed; application dismissed. On s.387(d): no evidence of a refusal — Nuvei told Mr Riley he could bring a support person to each meeting and he did — and the submission that an 'imbalance of arms' from in-house counsel attending was itself relevant to s.387(d) was rejected as misconceived.

[2022] FWC 1439.outcome: Found not to have been unfairly dismissed; application dismissed. On s.387(d): the Applicant attended the show-cause meeting with his paid agent, so the Commission treated the factor as neutral. An earlier consultation letter (for a different, earlier meeting) had told the Applicant his support person could not ask questions or advocate on his behalf.

[2023] FWC 793.outcome: Found not to have been unfairly dismissed; application dismissed. On s.387(d): the Respondent's show-cause letter told the Applicant she could bring a support person, and there was no evidence of any refusal.

[2023] FWC 2485.short_name: Wang v Perfect Shape Medical Beauty Australia
[2023] FWC 2485.outcome: Found to have been unfairly dismissed; compensation of $4,312 ordered. On s.387(d): the Commission accepted the Applicant's unchallenged and unexplored assertion that her request for a support person was refused, and found that refusal unreasonable.

[2023] FWC 3399.outcome: Found to have been unfairly dismissed; compensation ordered. On s.387(d): the Commission found Adcon did unreasonably refuse a support person — it refused Mr Vonja's request that the dismissal discussion continue in the site office where his union representative was located.

[2022] FWC 1966.short_name: Szkwarek v Omega Network Pty Ltd
[2022] FWC 1966.outcome: Application dismissed — the dismissal was not harsh, unjust or unreasonable, confirmed at [100]. On s.387(e), the Commission found the applicant's lateness, failure to notify and failure to attend a disciplinary meeting were matters of conduct rather than performance, so whether he had been warned about unsatisfactory performance was not a relevant consideration — confirmed at [84] (the Commission went on to find, in the alternative, that he had in fact been warned).

[2022] FWC 520.short_name: Yap v Club Assist Pty Ltd
[2022] FWC 520.outcome: No valid reason for dismissal found; the dismissal was held to be unjust and unreasonable and the applicant was reinstated under s.391(1)(a), with continuity of employment and lost remuneration orders — confirmed at [78]-[79]. On s.387(e), the Commission held that the warning letter relied on by the employer did not constitute a warning about unsatisfactory performance for the purposes of s.387(e), because (among other things) it was merely exhortatory and did not identify with precision what the employee needed to do to improve — confirmed at [51]-[53].

[2024] FWC 1449.short_name: Mustafa v Core Service Holdings Pty Ltd
[2024] FWC 1449.outcome: Dismissal found harsh, unjust and unreasonable — confirmed at [30]; compensation of four weeks' pay ($5,261.44 gross) ordered — confirmed at [44]. On s.387(e), the Commission found there was no evidence the applicant was warned about any alleged performance issues or advised that his employment was at risk — confirmed at [26].

[2024] FWC 2078.short_name: Taylor v CJD Equipment Pty Ltd
[2024] FWC 2078.outcome: Application dismissed — the applicant's dismissal was not unfair, confirmed at [139]. On s.387(e), the Commission found the written performance warnings had a sufficient nexus to the underperformance ultimately relied on for dismissal (continuing KPI and sales-target concerns raised in writing), satisfying s.387(e) — confirmed at [131].

[2020] FWC 416.short_name: Zhao v University of Technology Sydney
[2020] FWC 416.outcome: Dismissal found 'harsh and unreasonable' — confirmed at [120]. The 'harsh' finding rested on s.387(h) mitigating factors: 14 years of otherwise unblemished service, the career damage of a performance dismissal, very limited alternative employment prospects, and sole caring responsibility for elderly parents plus a mortgage — confirmed at [119]. Reinstatement, continuity of service and lost remuneration ordered — confirmed at [136]-[137]. Permission to appeal was later refused by a Full Bench majority (see [2020] FWCFB 3571), so these orders stood.

[2020] FWCFB 3571.short_name: University of Technology Sydney v Zhao
[2020] FWCFB 3571.outcome: Full Bench majority (Catanzariti VP and Johns C) refused the University's permission to appeal — confirmed at [65]-[66]. Deputy President Colman dissented and would have granted permission, upheld the appeal and quashed the decision, but this was not the majority view, so Dr Zhao's reinstatement at first instance stood.

[2021] FWC 1229.short_name: Gagulich v Cardio Respiratory Sleep Pty Ltd
[2021] FWC 1229.outcome: Dismissal found unjust and unfair — confirmed at [98]-[99] — because Ms Gagulich was not notified of, nor given a reasonable opportunity to respond to, certain reasons relied on for her dismissal. This was despite a valid reason being found, and despite the Commission finding the dismissal proportionate to her proven conduct under s.387(h) — confirmed at [95]. CRS's small size and lack of an HR function were accepted but found not to weigh in the harsh/unjust/unreasonable assessment under ss.387(f)-(g) — confirmed at [92]-[93].

[2020] FWC 2819.short_name: Bertos v Northern NSW Football Limited
[2020] FWC 2819.outcome: Application dismissed — the dismissal was found not harsh, unjust or unreasonable, confirmed at [76]-[77]. The Commission rejected Mr Bertos's s.387(h) comparative-unfairness argument because none of his comparator examples were properly comparable — confirmed at [69] — applying the Full Bench's test (quoting Darvell v Australian Postal Corporation, in turn quoting Sexton v Pacific National and Daly v Bendigo Health Care Group) that there must be sufficient evidence of the allegedly comparable cases — confirmed at [67]-[68]. The proportionality of the summary dismissal was weighed against the gravity of the conduct — confirmed at [70] — and Mr Bertos's personal and economic circumstances (married, young family, COVID-affected job search) were considered under s.387(h) but did not outweigh that gravity — confirmed at [74].

[2020] FWC 4929.short_name: Jackson v Botanical Cuisine Pty Ltd
[2020] FWC 4929.outcome: Dismissal found harsh, unjust and unreasonable; Ms Jackson unfairly dismissed — confirmed at [14]. The employer's small size and lack of HR specialists were found, under ss.387(f)-(g), to have had an adverse effect on the (minimal) procedures followed — confirmed at [13] — but this did not excuse the outcome.

[2023] FWC 927.short_name: Coorey v Australia Tile Wholesale Pty Ltd
[2023] FWC 927.outcome: Mr Coorey found unfairly dismissed — confirmed at [28]. A valid reason existed, but the dismissal was unreasonable because it was entirely lacking in procedural fairness — confirmed at [28]. The Commission found the employer's small size (no HR or specialist expertise) and the personal (rather than professional) nature of the relationship between the two men likely explained the absence of any procedure, under ss.387(f)-(g) — confirmed at [25] — but, again, this did not excuse the lack of fairness.

[2021] FWC 5905.short_name: Rezaeifard v Green Leaves ELC Pty Ltd
[2021] FWC 5905.outcome: No valid reason for dismissal found — confirmed at [132]; dismissal found harsh, unjust and unreasonable — confirmed at [139]; compensation ordered. Because the employer was a large organisation with a dedicated HR specialist, ss.387(f)-(g) did not operate to excuse its procedural failures — confirmed at [137]; the Commission clarified that ss.387(f)-(g) test only the presence or absence of HR expertise, not whether that expertise was well used — confirmed at [124]-[125]. Proportionality was framed by quoting the Byrne v Australian Airlines Ltd formulation that a dismissal may be harsh because it is disproportionate to the gravity of the misconduct — confirmed at [85].

[2021] FWC 2203.short_name: Longobardi v New Horizons Enterprises Limited
[2021] FWC 2203.outcome: Application dismissed — dismissal found not harsh, unjust or unreasonable — confirmed at [92]-[93]. A valid reason was found, and the employer (a substantial enterprise with its own HR employees, so ss.387(f)-(g) were neutral — confirmed at [81]-[83]) was found to have conducted a fair and impartial investigation when the applicant challenged its quality as an 'other relevant matter' under s.387(h) — confirmed at [84]-[85]. The summary nature of the dismissal was weighed against the gravity of the conduct under s.387(h) — confirmed at [88].

[2025] FWC 3826.outcome: Dismissal found harsh, unjust and unreasonable. The investigator's finding on one allegation changed from unsubstantiated to substantiated, and the recommendation from a warning to termination, after the decision-maker pushed back and the complainant's mother applied pressure — confirmed at [52]-[53]. The Commission found the decision-maker did not make a proper or fair assessment of the evidence — confirmed at [58]. Final finding that the employer did not comply with its obligation to act fairly and impartially in the disciplinary procedure — confirmed at [62]. Briginshaw standard noted at [14]; preference for live evidence over a written account at [31].

[2021] FWC 2243.outcome: Application dismissed — valid reason found related to conduct, notwithstanding that the external investigator had restricted the investigation's scope and had not fully considered the employee's response to the draft report before finalising it, confirmed at [140]-[142]. A claim that the investigation was tainted merely because one manager had also been involved in an earlier, separate investigation was rejected for lack of evidence of actual partiality, confirmed at [146]. The Commission held that imperfect findings in an investigation report do not automatically invalidate the whole process where a valid reason is otherwise independently supported by other evidence, confirmed at [152]. Valid reason found at [153]. Final order (application dismissed) at [225].

[2021] FWCFB 6018.outcome: Full Bench appeal from [2021] FWC 2243. Permission to appeal refused — the Full Bench found the matter turned on its own facts and that the Commissioner's decision was open to her on the material before her, and did not raise any matter of importance or general application; confirmed at [40]. [2021] FWC 2243 was left undisturbed.

[2023] FWC 1198.short_name: Bowen v Cape York Grassroots Aboriginal Corporation
[2023] FWC 1198.outcome: Application dismissed — not unfair. The Commission held the employer bears the onus of proving misconduct on the balance of probabilities in accordance with Briginshaw v Briginshaw, such that 'reasonable satisfaction' is not produced by inexact proofs, indefinite testimony or indirect inferences, confirmed at [81]. Found the allegations had been notified with sufficient detail to allow a response, confirmed at [60]. Found the conduct (misrepresenting grant approval) made out but not accompanied by evidence of related fraud, applying Briginshaw to scope the finding, confirmed at [90]. Final finding (not harsh, unjust or unreasonable) at [132], order dismissing the application at [134].

[2024] FWC 2914.outcome: Dismissal found harsh, unjust and unreasonable — no valid reason established. The employer's investigators elected not to speak to a key witness and relied solely on their own analysis of an email, leaving them without a sufficiently reliable counterfactual to find the employee had made a false denial, confirmed at [162]. Finding that misconduct was not established to the requisite standard on the balance of probabilities, confirmed at [140]. Final finding of unfairness at [168] and [229]; compensation of $25,773.82 ordered at [231].

[2022] FWC 221.outcome: Application dismissed — not unfair, after 35 years' service. The allegations put to the employee at the investigation meeting specified the date, approximate time, location, the precise physical conduct alleged and its approximate duration, confirmed at [100]. Final finding (not harsh, unjust or unreasonable) at [286], order dismissing the application at [287].

[2022] FWC 1774.short_name: CFMMEU v British Concrete Pty Ltd
[2022] FWC 1774.outcome: The Commission found British Concrete never stood Mr Salha down, nor purported to, under s.524 — his absence from work stemmed from his non-compliance with a vaccination direction, not from any of the s.524(1) causes — so the Union had no standing to bring a s.526 dispute on his behalf. Application dismissed.

[2024] FWC 3306.outcome: The Commission found the mine's month-long stand down was authorised under s.524(1)(c): there was a genuine stoppage of work caused by a regulator's Prohibition Notice, the employees could not be usefully employed, and Wollongong Resources had taken reasonable steps in response such that it could not reasonably be held responsible for the stoppage. Dispute application dismissed.

[2025] FWCFB 274.short_name: ANMF v St Vincent's Private Hospitals (Full Bench)
[2025] FWCFB 274.outcome: On appeal, the Full Bench held the Commissioner erred: an employee's refusal of available redeployment work, made as protected industrial action, is not the same as having no useful work 'because of' industrial action under s.524(1)(a) — s.524 concerns an absence of work, not an employee's unwillingness to perform available work. The stand down was not authorised by s.524(1)(a). On redetermination, the Full Bench still declined to order payment on fairness grounds under s.526(4), for different reasons than the Commissioner gave. Permission to appeal granted; appeal dismissed.

[2025] FWC 1441.outcome: This is a jurisdictional decision only, on whether Mr Poulter was 'dismissed' within s.386(1)(a) — the underlying unfair dismissal merits were not decided here. The Commission found JA Concreting's withholding of work and pay was authorised neither by Mr Poulter's contract of employment nor by s.524 (none of the s.524(1) causes were shown), so it was not a lawful stand down. By filing his unfair dismissal application, Mr Poulter accepted this repudiation, and his employment was found to have been terminated at his employer's initiative under s.386(1)(a). The objection to the application was dismissed.

[2020] FWC 1461.outcome: In a s.739 dispute under the University's enterprise agreement, the Commission found the University had grounds, under the agreement's own two-step suspension clause (first, whether the misconduct allegation was serious enough to warrant the employee not being at work; second, whether that suspension should be paid or unpaid), to commence serious misconduct proceedings and to suspend Mr Kerig without pay while it did so, and had complied with the agreement's procedure.

[2022] FWC 1530.outcome: Cited here only for a letter reproduced in the decision, in which the applicant's representative quoted Avenia v Railway & Transport Health Fund Ltd [2017] FCA 859 at [154] on the common law position on suspension without pay. This decision's own finding concerned an unrelated vaccination-mandate dismissal and is not relied on here — not asserted as this decision's holding.

[2021] FWC 6329.short_name: Lakhan v Bus Tech (SA) Pty Ltd
[2021] FWC 6329.outcome: The Commission found Mr Lakhan's dismissal was harsh and unjust, and therefore unfair. Cited here for its reasoning on how the absence of a contemporaneous documentary record, and the self-serving potential of a senior manager's evidence, limited what factual findings could be made about disputed workplace conversations.

[2023] FWC 276.short_name: Clark v Reliable Signs and Refinishing
[2023] FWC 276.outcome: The Commission found there was no valid reason for Mr Clark's dismissal. Cited here because the employer could point to no documented information — written or oral — recording any warning given to the Applicant, and its own witness's oral evidence was found to go beyond what was in his written statement.

[2022] FWC 2455.short_name: Green v Citic Pacific Mining Management Pty Ltd
[2022] FWC 2455.outcome: The Commission found Mr Green's dismissal was not, in an objective sense, unfair. Cited here because it was the employee's own account of a conversation — inconsistent with his manager's contemporaneous diary note — that was rejected as self-serving, showing the documentary-record principle cuts against whichever party lacks the record, not only employers.

[2025] FWC 3513.short_name: ASU and RTBU v Queensland Rail Transit Authority
[2025] FWC 3513.outcome: This is a s.739 enterprise-bargaining dispute, not an unfair dismissal matter, so it is cited only for its restatement of the general evidentiary principle that the Commission prefers documentary evidence to oral recollection where a dispute arises after the fact — and because the Commission applied that principle to find no agreement had in fact been reached on the disputed monetary value. The balance of the arbitrated outcome (board-trigger numbers, implementation detail) was not reviewed and is not relied on here.

[2023] FWC 1502.short_name: Durmic v Department of Home Affairs
[2023] FWC 1502.outcome: Permission to be represented by a lawyer granted to the Department of Home Affairs under s.596(2)(a) (efficiency, given the complexity of the jurisdictional objection) and the Commission separately found it would also have been unfair not to allow representation under s.596(2)(b) if (a) had not been made out. Confirmed at [28], [30], [53], [54].

[2021] FWC 6336.short_name: Donnola v Silverleaf Constructions Co Pty Ltd
[2021] FWC 6336.outcome: Permission to be represented refused. The applicant's lawyer had been acting since the dispute arose and the applicant said he lacked legal training, but the Commission found no demonstrated complexity under s.596(2)(a) and no unfairness made out under s.596(2)(b) or (c) — lack of legal training alone is not enough. Confirmed at [19], [22], [28], [30]-[31], [35].

[2021] FWC 526.short_name: Petersen v Kizuri Capital Pty Ltd (T/A Allpet Products)
[2021] FWC 526.outcome: Confirmed: this is a standalone costs decision setting out the s.400A and s.611 statutory tests and the 'basic rule' that each party bears its own costs, with costs under those sections being the exception ([55]-[58]). Confirmed the Commission rejected the s.611(2) 'no reasonable prospect of success' ground against the respondent's defence of the substantive claim ([70]). This pass did NOT confirm the final costs order/quantum: the decision's own concluding paragraphs ([131]-[134], where a s.400A costs order for $3,947.05 over unanswered settlement offers was in fact made per the raw reconstructed text) sit beyond a paragraph-numbering gap in this corpus pass and could not be resolved through the standard paragraph reconstruction tool, so no pinpoint cite is made to that part of the outcome.

[2020] FWC 316.short_name: Cowper v Trustees of Edmund Rice Education Australia (T/A St Joseph's Flexible Learning Centre)
[2020] FWC 316.outcome: Costs application under s.400A and s.611 dismissed; no order for costs made. The respondent's vigorous but genuine defence of a factually disputed matter, and its reasoned non-acceptance of settlement offers, were not an unreasonable act or omission, and it was not reasonably apparent the defence had no reasonable prospects of success. Confirmed at [58], [60]-[62], [67]-[68], [80]-[82].

[2020] FWC 2491.short_name: McCaffery v Kizuri Capital Pty Ltd / WS Partners Unit Trust (T/A Warren Smith & Partners)
[2020] FWC 2491.outcome: Confirmed: the respondent's own s.611/s.400A costs application against the applicant (seeking $29,578.34) was dismissed in full — the vexatious-application claim was abandoned at hearing and no unreasonable act or omission by the applicant was established ([66]). The applicant's reciprocal costs application against the respondent then succeeded in part: because the respondent's 'vexatious application' head of claim had, on the facts known to it, no reasonable prospect of success and was pursued without reasonable cause, the Commission ordered the respondent to pay the applicant's costs of that part of the cross-claim on an indemnity basis, while rejecting the applicant's claim on the s.400A limb ([71], [73], [75]). The precise quantum/apportionment of that final costs order ([76]-[77]) was left to the parties to agree and is not asserted here.

[2020] FWC 1181.short_name: Bell v Singaria (Aust) Pty Ltd (T/A Crown on McCredie)
[2020] FWC 1181.outcome: A conciliation conference resulted in an agreed settlement (monetary payment plus resignation and a statement of service), with the cooling-off period waived. The applicant later tried to resile from it, but the Commission found a binding settlement had been reached and dismissed the unfair dismissal application under s.587(1)(c) as having no reasonable prospects of success. Confirmed at [5]-[9], [47]-[48].

[2023] FWC 2900.short_name: Lee v Hybrid PG Pty Ltd atf Hybrid Property Group
[2023] FWC 2900.outcome: Dismissal found harsh, unjust and unreasonable — confirmed at [112]. Reinstatement found inappropriate — confirmed at [118]. Compensation of $6,386.28 assessed over a 6-week anticipated employment period, reduced by one week ($1,064.38) for inadequate mitigation, not affected by the compensation cap, and ordered at $5,321.90 plus superannuation — confirmed at [127]-[129], [137]-[141].

[2026] FWC 2050.short_name: Allouche v Skyco Group Pty Ltd
[2026] FWC 2050.outcome: Dismissal found unfair (unreasonable for lack of notice/opportunity to respond, and harsh given personal circumstances) — confirmed at [44]. Reinstatement found inappropriate because the applicant did not seek it, had found new work, and the valid reason involved threats against remaining staff — confirmed at [46]. Compensation found appropriate in principle but reduced to nil under s.392(3) because the applicant's own conduct contributed to the dismissal — confirmed at [48]-[49].

[2020] FWC 4840.short_name: Thurston v Bunbury Medical Imaging Pty Ltd
[2020] FWC 4840.outcome: Reinstatement found inappropriate due to a mutual, soundly-based loss of trust and confidence between the applicant and the practice owner — confirmed at [3], [7]-[8]. The first-instance compensation calculation (nil payable, confirmed at [38]) was overturned on appeal in [2021] FWCFB 280 for misapplying the Sprigg formula; this module relies only on the reinstatement-inappropriate reasoning (which the Full Bench left undisturbed) and uses the compensation calculation as a worked illustration of how that step can go wrong, not as a correct final figure.

[2021] FWCFB 280.short_name: Thurston v Bunbury Medical Imaging Pty Ltd (appeal)
[2021] FWCFB 280.outcome: Permission to appeal granted; the appeal succeeded only on the compensation calculation, which the Full Bench found misapplied the Sprigg formula by offsetting the applicant's full post-dismissal earnings against the full anticipated employment period rather than the shortfall between the two — confirmed at [30], [32], [34]. The appeal was otherwise dismissed (the reinstatement-inappropriate finding was not disturbed). Corrected compensation of $7,029.90 inclusive of superannuation was ordered — confirmed at [36], [40].

[2020] FWC 2.outcome: Application dismissed under s.587(1)(c) for want of reasonable prospects of success — confirmed at [36]: the applicant had signed a Deed of Release on redundancy, the Commission found no duress in the signing, and the Deed barred the unfair dismissal claim. Cited here for [6], where the Commission records that it granted the respondent's lawyer permission to appear only after being satisfied the requirements of s.596(2)(a) of the FW Act were met; the unrepresented applicant had no equivalent permission to seek. Used to illustrate that legal or paid-agent representation in a Commission matter is not automatic, and that its presence on the other side is itself an escalation trigger.

[2022] FWC 103.outcome: Read start to finish. Mr Roach, a train driver, smoked cannabis on a day off and returned a positive urine test for cannabinoids two days later in a safety-critical rail role. The Commission accepted he may not have felt impaired but held that did not establish he was not in fact impaired, found a valid reason in simply attending work with a proscribed level of cannabinoids in his system (not in his being discernibly affected), found he had an independent notification obligation he breached, and found the dismissal was not unfair.

[2023] FWC 2465.outcome: Read start to finish. Mr Haigh, an MPU operator handling explosives at a mine, was prescribed medicinal cannabis, disclosed it once, then resumed using it after stopping an alternative medication without re-disclosing, which only came to light after a post-incident test. The Commission found a valid reason in the non-disclosure itself — holding that policy language like "could impair" and "may affect" captures the possibility of impairment regardless of whether actual impairment is proven — but found the dismissal was not harsh, unjust or unreasonable overall and dismissed the application, despite accepting he had passed every drug test.

[2024] FWC 2154.outcome: Read the valid-reason reasoning in detail (a very long decision; not every paragraph was read). A cabin crew member had a glass of prosecco 7.5 hours before signing on, inside Virgin's 8-hour alcohol rule, after checking with a manager and breathalysing himself. The Commission found he had technically breached the rule but that Virgin's drug and alcohol policy material was spread inconsistently across multiple manuals and communicated with conflicting messaging about whether the 8-hour rule was binding, found no valid reason for the dismissal, found it harsh in any event, and ordered reinstatement.

[2020] FWC 250.outcome: Valid reason found: a course of safety-related misconduct over several years in which the Applicant (a 30-year driver/glass worker) repeatedly failed to comply with safety policies and procedures, confirmed at [142]. Long service and age weighed towards harshness but were outweighed by the criticality of safety in a high-risk work environment, confirmed at [176]. Application dismissed, confirmed at [177].

[2020] FWC 120.outcome: Valid reason found at [140] (repeated, deliberate breach of a pedestrian-walkway safety rule plus other misconduct). The Respondent's past inconsistent enforcement of the walkway rule was found relevant and weighed somewhat towards unfairness, confirmed at [129]-[130] and [156], but was not enough to outweigh the other factors. Application for an unfair dismissal remedy dismissed, confirmed at [163].

[2021] FWC 838.outcome: Valid reason found (breach of a mine's Safehaven Rules, described as a 'near miss'), confirmed at [148]-[149]. Despite the valid reason, the dismissal was found harsh, unjust and unreasonable because the Applicant was treated more severely than colleagues involved in an actual, more serious collision, confirmed at [152] and [156].

[2022] FWC 1522.outcome: Dismissal of a 12-year electricity-network crew leader upheld following an incident in which a customer received an electric shock (actual harm, not a near miss). His seniority/leadership role at the time was treated as an aggravating factor that justified harsher treatment than other employees investigated over the same incident, confirmed at [231]. His honest, responsibility-accepting Show Cause response was credited but not decisive, confirmed at [232]. Application dismissed, confirmed at [239].

[2020] FWC 3924.outcome: No valid reason found. A 30-year warehouse operator was dismissed after a low-severity tugger collision with no injury or property damage; the Commission found the incident did not justify dismissal, partly because the other driver was also at fault and travelling against the one-way rule, confirmed at [196]-[197] and [220]. The Commission rejected a blanket consistency argument (comparator incidents were materially different) but accepted the comparison with the other driver in the same incident was not probative either way given his shorter service and clean record, confirmed at [211] and [213]. The Commission separately observed that long service in one role can itself breed complacency and is no excuse for safety breaches, confirmed at [243]. Applicant reinstated.

[2023] FWC 1997.outcome: The Commission set out the legal meaning of sexual harassment in s.28A of the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth) — confirmed at [62] — and found that Mr Swift sexually harassed three colleagues over an extended period — confirmed at [67]. The Commission held sexual harassment is conduct that will ordinarily justify dismissal, and that an employer's positive duty to eliminate sexual harassment applied to the respondent at the time of the dismissal — confirmed at [68]. Intent and consent were held irrelevant to whether the conduct was sexual harassment — confirmed at [69]-[70]. The application was dismissed; the dismissal was not unfair — confirmed at [93]-[94].

[2024] FWC 2731.outcome: The Commission applied the employer's sexual-harassment definition (mirroring s.28A SDA) and found, on the balance of probabilities, that the Applicant's conduct on a flight constituted sexual harassment and a separate incident constituted (non-sexual) harassment — confirmed at [145], [150], [152] and [154]. The Commission noted the employer's submission about its legislated positive duty to eliminate sexual harassment — confirmed at [155] — and found a valid reason for dismissal — confirmed at [156]. The application was dismissed; the dismissal was not unfair.

[2024] FWC 2062.outcome: The Commission found the Applicant's conduct towards two colleagues was sexual harassment and that this gave the Respondent a valid reason to terminate — confirmed at [160]. The Respondent had submitted its action was consistent with its positive duty to prevent or eliminate workplace sexual harassment under the SDA — confirmed at [106]. Despite the valid reason, the Commission found the dismissal process was rushed purely for administrative convenience (an impending mine ownership transfer and an Easter long weekend), denying the Applicant a full opportunity to respond, and held the dismissal unfair overall — confirmed at [181]-[182].

[2026] FWC 1551.outcome: This is an enterprise-agreement dispute under s.739 of the FW Act about an employer's handling of a sexual harassment complaint — not an unfair dismissal matter. It is cited here only for its explanation, drawn from the Revised Explanatory Memorandum to the Respect at Work reforms, of the purpose of the positive duty inserted into the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth) — confirmed at [29]. The Commission's ultimate findings on Metro's compliance with the enterprise agreement clause were not read in this pass and nothing about them is asserted here.

[2025] FWC 2853.outcome: The Commission found the evidence did not establish that Mr Walsh's conduct was repeated and unreasonable, or that it created a risk to health and safety, and so it did not rise to workplace bullying (a single heated, in-the-moment incident was not enough) — confirmed at [176]. The Commission was also not satisfied the conduct was discriminatory or constituted sexual harassment, and found no valid reason for the dismissal — confirmed at [177]-[178]. The dismissal was found unfair; reinstatement, continuity of service and compensation were ordered.

[2024] FWC 3231.outcome: Mr Bale sent emails to a colleague that were, on their face, belittling and insulting — confirmed at [2]. The Commission found this conduct was serious and self-evidently a valid reason for dismissal — confirmed at [109]. The application was dismissed; the dismissal was not unfair — confirmed at [110]-[111].

[2024] FWC 2115.short_name: Pawelczyk v Commonwealth Bank of Australia
[2024] FWC 2115.outcome: Mr Pawelczyk sent more than 50 messages to his manager over six days; the Commission found it did not matter whether he intended to cause harm, and that the messages were deliberate and targeted — confirmed at [11]. The Commission found a valid reason for the dismissal — confirmed at [56] — and that the dismissal process was fair. The dismissal was not unfair.

[2020] FWC 3684.outcome: Deputy President Dean applied the three-part inherent-requirements test (quoting a Full Bench) and found a valid reason for dismissal related to capacity: the applicant was not capable of performing the inherent requirements of her role at the time of dismissal, was unlikely to be able to do so in the foreseeable future, and no reasonable adjustment could accommodate her incapacity. Confirmed at [66]-[67] and [73].

[2022] FWC 1871.outcome: Application dismissed. The Commission found a valid reason for dismissal based on the applicant's inability, confirmed by an unchallenged independent medical (Fitness For Duty) report, to safely perform the inherent requirements of a Receivables Forklift Operator role, now or into the future, and found no reasonable work adjustment could overcome the restrictions. Confirmed at [33]-[43] and [67]-[68].

[2022] FWC 786.outcome: Application dismissed. The Commission gave substantial weight to the consistent, long-term view of the applicant's treating GP (who saw him most frequently) that he was permanently restricted from working with his supervisor, found a proposed reasonable adjustment (reporting-line change) was in substance unworkable, and found a valid reason for dismissal related to capacity. Confirmed at [220]-[221]; the quoted inherent-requirements principle from X v Commonwealth is confirmed at [103].

[2023] FWC 1125.outcome: Application dismissed. The Commission found a valid reason for dismissal related to capacity, found the company had afforded the applicant a reasonable opportunity to recover (almost three months, with no reasonable basis to expect imminent improvement) before dismissing him, and explained that two apparently conflicting fitness-for-duty reports were not truly in conflict because they were commissioned by different entities for different purposes. Confirmed at [15]-[16], [20], [23] and [27].

[2024] FWC 880.short_name: Thomas v Oz Design Furniture Ballina
[2024] FWC 880.outcome: Application dismissed. Applying the three-part inherent-requirements test to an employee on a progressively reducing return-to-work schedule after a serious car accident, the Commission found a valid reason for dismissal related to capacity. Procedural deficiencies (no prior notification or opportunity to respond) added weight to a finding of unfairness but were ultimately outweighed by the strength of the capacity evidence and the employer's patience in keeping the role open. Confirmed at [52]-[55], [68] and [71].

[2020] FWC 5557.outcome: Confirmed only for the proposition that dismissal for inability to perform the inherent requirements of a role "within a reasonable time frame" is a capacity-related reason, and that on these facts (over 12 months' absence, no medical evidence of an end point) the Commission found a valid reason for dismissal related to capacity at [68]. This decision's overall conclusion on harshness (the Commission's remarks at [94] indicate the dismissal was ultimately found unfair) was not independently traced in this pass -- it appears to turn on separate notice-entitlement findings around [90]-[93] that this pass did not fully reconstruct. Do not rely on this entry for the overall outcome.

[2023] FWC 2906.outcome: Application dismissed. The applicant had been absent for over two years with an unchanged prognosis and repeatedly failed to comply with lawful and reasonable directions to attend an independent medical examination. The Commission found those IME directions lawful and reasonable and the applicant's non-compliance (together with the underlying medical evidence) a valid reason for dismissal. Confirmed at [93], [97]-[101] and [136].

[2026] FWC 554.outcome: Application dismissed. The applicant conceded he could not perform the inherent requirements of his role at the date of dismissal; the Commission found this, confirmed by consistent medical evidence of total and likely permanent incapacity, a valid reason for dismissal. The Commission rejected arguments that the employer should instead have pursued early-intervention rehabilitation, extended leave without pay, or redeployment, finding none of those options were relevant to valid reason or made the dismissal unfair on the facts. Confirmed at [35], [54], [56]-[57], [59] and [61].

[2025] FWC 2226.outcome: Found two valid reasons for dismissal under s.387(a): persistent absenteeism (92 days of absence in the prior year) meaning Mr Clark was not meeting the inherent requirement of attending for work, and repeated failure to follow lawful and reasonable directions to notify the company of absences and provide supporting medical evidence. Held the dismissal was not harsh, unjust or unreasonable; application dismissed. Note: the decision itself records that an appeal under s.604 (C2025/8102) was lodged against it — this entry reflects the first-instance findings only.

[2021] FWC 1217.outcome: On two specific absence days taken close to a period of authorised, certified sick leave, the Commission found no valid reason even though no medical certificate covered those exact two days. But a separate instance of turning up 1.5 hours late with no claimed illness, injury or emergency was found to be a valid reason. Taking the whole s.387 analysis together (including two prior written warnings), the dismissal overall was found not harsh, unjust or unreasonable and the application was dismissed.

[2023] FWC 2471.outcome: Jurisdictional hearing only. The employer argued the employee had abandoned his employment on one of three alternative dates while on a workers' compensation absence. The Commission held the employer never attempted to contact the employee to check its suspicion, and the employee's absence was fully explained by his ongoing, employer-acknowledged workers' compensation incapacity and rehabilitation plan. Found the employee did not abandon his employment, but separately found there was also no dismissal by the employer (the employment relationship was still on foot) — so the unfair dismissal application was dismissed for want of a dismissal on either view.

[2025] FWC 3612.outcome: Jurisdictional decision on whether there was a dismissal and whether the application was in time. The employer had a reasonable basis to suspect abandonment after the employee failed to return from overseas leave as planned, but the Commission held it was incumbent on the employer to confirm this with the employee before acting on that belief, which it did not do. Found the employee was dismissed when later removed from the staff rostering chat; jurisdictional objections (including abandonment) dismissed. This decision addresses jurisdiction only, not the eventual merits of the unfair dismissal claim.

[2021] FWC 6333.short_name: Fathers v Global Line Marking Services
[2021] FWC 6333.outcome: A general protections dismissal dispute under s.365 (which uses the same s.386 definition of dismissal). The employee missed five consecutive rostered shifts without advising anyone in advance, despite a manager's attempt to reach him. The Commission found the employee abandoned his employment, so there was no dismissal at the employer's initiative within the meaning of s.386; the application was dismissed.

[2021] FWC 2322.outcome: The employee stopped responding to the employer after his last certified sick leave period expired, including not replying to a letter warning that continued silence would be treated as abandonment. Weeks later he resigned, then brought an unfair dismissal claim. The Commission found his conduct manifested a decision to abandon his employment, so he was not dismissed within the meaning of s.386; the jurisdictional objection was upheld and the application was dismissed.

[2023] FWC 907.short_name: Pelly v Ventia Australia Pty Ltd
[2023] FWC 907.outcome: Valid reason found for two policy breaches arising from posts in a private Facebook/messenger group (a disrespectful on-shift post about management, and an unauthorised base photo) — confirmed at [120]-[121]. But overall dismissal found harsh/unreasonable because of a haphazard notification process and differential treatment of a comparable colleague; the Applicant was reinstated with partial backpay — confirmed at [122]-[123], [157]-[161]. Upheld on appeal: the Full Bench recorded that the Commissioner had found a valid reason but still found the dismissal unjust and unreasonable, and dismissed Ventia's appeal — confirmed against [2023] FWCFB 201 at [2] (and, independently read, at its final orders).

[2023] FWCFB 201.short_name: Ventia Australia Pty Ltd v Pelly
[2023] FWCFB 201.outcome: Full Bench granted permission to appeal but dismissed the appeal, recording that the Commissioner had found a valid reason but still concluded the dismissal was unjust and unreasonable — confirmed at [2] and, independently read in the final paragraphs of the decision, at its concluding orders (permission to appeal granted; appeal dismissed). Note: a known corpus chunking defect causes an automated paragraph lookup for "[132]" in this decision to land on an earlier, unrelated reference to paragraph [132] of the first-instance decision rather than this Full Bench's own final order — for that reason only [2] is used as a <Cite> pinpoint; the final-order text was confirmed by direct reading, not via an automated-safe pinpoint.

[2021] FWC 3030.short_name: Waddy v Ability Centre Australasia Ltd
[2021] FWC 3030.outcome: Valid reason found: the Applicant's own public Facebook posts (racist comments about Aboriginal people) breached a Social Media Policy whose scope the Commission found did not overreach, because the Applicant had identified himself as the Respondent's employee on his profile and the posts were visible to the general public. Dismissal found not harsh, unjust or unreasonable — confirmed at [36], [38], [43]-[47] and [69].

[2021] FWC 2570.outcome: Valid reason found: the Applicant posted a sexually explicit meme referencing a female colleague to his personal, public Facebook page, then a second (arguably retaliatory) meme. The Commission rejected the argument that a "robust" sales-floor culture excused the conduct, finding it plainly inappropriate and sufficiently serious to justify dismissal; the dismissal was found neither harsh nor unjust — confirmed at [254], [256]-[257] and [266]-[267].

[2021] FWC 1952.short_name: Besanko v R.B. Aquatics Pty Ltd T/A Swimmers
[2021] FWC 1952.outcome: No valid reason found. The Applicant, a swim instructor, posted a competing swim school's name in reply to a stranger's request in a private, 16,100-member community Facebook group; a colleague who saw the post via her own notifications screenshotted it and forwarded it to management despite both women's profiles being set to private. The Commission found the private settings meant readers could not have told the Applicant worked for the Respondent, so there was no demonstrated connection to the employment sufficient to found a valid reason, and the summary dismissal was also not consistent with the Small Business Fair Dismissal Code. Dismissal found unfair; reinstatement found inappropriate; no compensation ordered because no loss was shown — confirmed at [12]-[13], [45]-[46], [52] and [99].

[2020] FWC 4819.short_name: Tiavo v Axiom Australia Pty Ltd
[2020] FWC 4819.outcome: The Commission rejected the applicant's claim that an incorrect timesheet entry was an innocent mistake, finding on the balance of probabilities (applying Briginshaw given the seriousness of a dishonesty finding) that he dishonestly entered his time. The dismissal was not harsh, unjust or unreasonable and the application was dismissed.

[2021] FWC 3224.short_name: Goburdhun v Endeavour Group Limited T/A BWS
[2021] FWC 3224.outcome: The Commission found the applicant deliberately and repeatedly falsified his clock-out times over eleven consecutive days to conceal that he was leaving work early, rejecting his explanation. This was serious misconduct and the dismissal was neither harsh, unjust nor unreasonable.

[2023] FWC 946.outcome: The Commission found the applicant was not honest in her dealings with the company, including representing by electronic records that she had attended participant appointments she had not, corroborated by multiple participants independently reporting the same thing. The company had good and substantiated reasons to dismiss her and the dismissal was not unfair.

[2026] FWC 2346.short_name: Petrie v Amazon Commercial Services Pty Ltd
[2026] FWC 2346.outcome: The Commission found the applicant's sign-off on a maintenance work order reflected an honest, but mistaken, understanding of what he had been authorised to do, not dishonesty or falsification. Overall the Commission was not satisfied the respondent had a valid reason for dismissal and ordered reinstatement.

[2021] FWC 6682.short_name: Stark v Charter Mercantile Agency Pty Ltd
[2021] FWC 6682.outcome: The Commission found it unnecessary to decide whether inaccurate timesheets were a deliberately deceitful act or reflected a genuine (if mistaken) belief about how to record hours worked, because the inaccuracy itself was a valid reason in a workplace that relied heavily on trust. Despite a procedural fairness failure, the dismissal was, on balance, not harsh, unjust or unreasonable.

[2024] FWC 311.short_name: Lainas v AMSPEC Australia Pty Ltd
[2024] FWC 311.outcome: The Commission found the applicant's 20 June 2022 timesheet claim for hours inconsistent with the company's recorded entry/exit times was a further valid reason for dismissal, alongside other conduct. Overall, however, the Commission found the dismissal was still harsh, unjust or unreasonable because of separate procedural failures, and reduced compensation by 30% on account of the applicant's misconduct. This entry confirms the timesheet finding and the overall unfair-dismissal/compensation-reduction outcome; the full multi-ground reasoning (covert recordings, abusive emails, notice issues) was not independently re-verified paragraph by paragraph.

[2024] FWC 1837.outcome: In an extension-of-time decision, the Commission found the applicant had misrepresented on his resume that he was a CA ANZ member when he was not, and commented in passing that the merits of his case were accordingly not strong. The application itself was dismissed for want of an extension of time, not on a final merits/valid-reason determination, so only the resume-misrepresentation finding is relied on here, not a concluded valid-reason outcome.

[2026] FWC 898.short_name: Bowen v Queensland Rail Transit Authority
[2026] FWC 898.outcome: Cited here only for its discussion, quoting a Full Bench decision in Newton v Toll Transport Pty Ltd, of Streeter v Telstra Corporation Limited: that an employee's dishonesty in interviews with their employer during an investigation can itself found a separate valid reason for dismissal, even where the underlying out-of-hours conduct does not. This decision's own facts and outcome (concerning undisclosed criminal charges) are not relied on and not asserted here.

[2021] FWC 6394.outcome: Cited here only for its statement of the general principle, drawing on APS Group (Placements) Pty Ltd v O'Loughlin, that after-acquired knowledge or evidence may strengthen an employer's valid-reason case while weakening its procedural-fairness case. This decision's own subject matter (a ruling on reopening evidence in an unrelated unfair dismissal matter) is not relied on and not asserted here.

[2025] FWC 3124.short_name: Sinclair v Transit Systems NSW Pty Ltd
[2025] FWC 3124.outcome: No contravention of Part 3-1 found — confirmed at [70]. The applicant did not identify the workplace law or instrument behind his alleged entitlements and did not establish a workplace right under s.341(1)(a), (b) or (c) ([57]); a workers compensation claim was likely to be a workplace right but was not exercised before dismissal ([58]).

[2023] FWC 245.short_name: Hodgkins v Rockcote Enterprises Pty Ltd
[2023] FWC 245.outcome: Read only for the workplace-right findings at [156] and [161]–[163]: one email was a mere request for assistance, not a complaint or inquiry; later emails were complaints or inquiries even though misconceived. The decision's ultimate finding and orders were not read in this pass — not asserted here.

[2026] FWC 1941.short_name: Barakat v Grimshaw Architects Pty Ltd
[2026] FWC 1941.outcome: Read only for the statement at [33] that there is no workplace right to have discussions or obtain clarification on the terms of an employment contract at the point of recruitment. The decision's ultimate finding was not read in this pass — not asserted here.

[2023] HCA 27.short_name: Qantas Airways Ltd v Transport Workers' Union of Australia
[2023] HCA 27.outcome: Appeal dismissed. Read directly for the s.340(1)(b) future-exercise proposition at [43] and [60].

[2023] FCA 1036.outcome: Fair Work Act claims dismissed — confirmed at [145]. A general counsel alleged she was made redundant because of two complaints and her sick leave. O'Callaghan J accepted the chief executive as a reliable witness ([121]) and that redundancy was the true and only reason ([133]). Direct source record: quoted phrases and paragraph numbers were confirmed on 13 November 2026 against the judgment file held in the Briefer corpus (collected from the Federal Court), not re-checked against the Court's website.

[2021] FCA 601.short_name: SBP Employment Solutions Pty Ltd v Smith
[2021] FCA 601.outcome: Appeal allowed in part — summary at [214]. Rangiah J held the primary judge misapplied Jones v Dunkel ([89]) but that the employer failed to prove the complaints were not a substantial and operative factor ([114]), so the s.340 contravention by the employer stood ([115]) and Ground 1 was rejected. Penalties and compensation were reduced, the declarations against two of the four directors were set aside, and the costs orders were replaced with no order as to costs.
